**Where we are ahead:** the most complete Zig CoAP: reliability, dedup, Block1/Block2 assembler and observe registry with RFC 7641 §7 notification budget (libcoap-style `COAP_OBS_MAX_NON` default), zero allocation, and real aiocoap datagram anchors; the only Zig CoAP found with observe and block-wise (cvik/coap not read: *(inferred)*). **Where we are behind:** no CoAP over WebSockets (RFC 8323 §4) and no RFC 7390 group-management resources (→ "What is deliberately not done"); the TCP/TLS framing and signaling, the multicast rules and combined Block1+Block2 are covered. The resource registry/dispatcher, CoRE link-format builder/parser with `.well-known/core` discovery, the named PATCH/FETCH/iPATCH codes, Echo/Request-Tag/No-Response options and RFC 8974 extended tokens are covered (see "Resources, link-format and RFC extras").

## Design & invariants
- **Layered, each independently testable:** `root` (C1) message codec — header/token/delta-encoded
  options/payload, `parse` (fills a caller option array; values borrow the datagram) /
  `serialize` (into a caller buffer) / `encodedLen`. `options` (C2) — the §5.10 option registry +
  §5.4.6 class bits + §3.2 CoAP-uint format + typed accessors + §6 URI↔options mapping.
  `reliability` (C3) — §4.2 CON retransmission with exponential backoff + deterministic jitter,
  §4.5 message-ID dedup window, empty-ACK/RST helpers. `client` (C4) — `buildRequest` +
  `Exchange.match` reply correlation. `server` (C5) — `isRequest` + piggyback/ackOnly/separate
  builders. `block` (C6, RFC 7959) — Block1/Block2 value codec (packed NUM:M:SZX), `split`,
  caller-storage `Assembler`. `observe` (C7, RFC 7641) — subscription `Registry` (Dedup-style
  bounded array + FIFO eviction), monotonic 24-bit `Sequence` + RFC 1982 lollipop `isNewer`; server
  push reuses `server.Server.separate` unchanged.
- **Zero-allocation, transport- and clock-agnostic:** codecs fill caller buffers; reliability and
  observe take the clock/sequence via caller state. Wire to any UDP/DTLS transport. Fully
  offline-testable.
- **Error policy:** malformed datagrams (bad TKL 9..15, option-number overflow, truncation, reserved
  SZX, oversized NUM) are typed errors, never panics.

## Resources, link-format and RFC extras

- **Resources and discovery** (`resource.zig`). `Registry.dispatch` routes by Uri-Path, checks the method, answers
  `/.well-known/core` from the registered resources (RFC 6690 §4, with the §4.1 filter) and honours No-Response
  (RFC 7967). A handler's `Reply` may also carry the Observe sequence number, a Block2 descriptor (and Size2) and a Block1
  descriptor to echo; the dispatcher writes them in option-number order.
- **Block-wise answers by the dispatcher** (RFC 7959 §2.4). `Resource.blockwise` serves the handler's whole payload in
  Block2 blocks: the block the request's Block2 names, or the first block (with Size2) when the payload exceeds
  `DispatchOptions.max_payload` (default 1024); a request that carries Block2 is always answered with a block. The
  server may answer a smaller size than asked (§2.3): the size is capped at what `max_payload` allows and NUM follows it.
  A block starting past the end, or a malformed Block2 value, is 4.02 Bad Option. The discovery document takes the same
  path; with `DispatchOptions.scratch` it is generated one link at a time per block, so it may be larger than `doc_buf`
  (which then only holds a block) and the document is counted for Size2. libcoap and go-coap serve a large
  `/.well-known/core` block-wise the same way.
- **Observe hook** (`Resource.observe_hook`, RFC 7641 §3.1). A GET with Observe 0 or 1 calls the hook (`register` /
  `deregister`) before the handler; the sequence number it returns becomes the response's Observe option (on 2.xx
  only). The hook owns the bookkeeping (e.g. an `observe.Registry` keyed by the request's token); other Observe values
  and non-GETs do not reach it.
- **Combined Block1+Block2** (`block.zig`, RFC 7959 §3.3). `Transfer` is the client state machine of one exchange whose
  request body goes out in Block1 blocks and whose response body arrives in Block2 blocks: Block2 rides on the request
  with the last Block1 block (and on the follow-up fetches, which carry no body), every Block1 acknowledgement is checked
  (NUM echoed), the first answer after the body is Block2 NUM 0 or the whole response. `Sender` carves a request body
  and follows a smaller size the peer names. The server side is the existing `Assembler` plus the dispatcher above.
- **SZX renegotiation** (RFC 7959 §2.3). A peer may continue at a smaller block size mid-transfer; `Assembler` and
  `Sender` take a smaller SZX at any block (NUM counted in the new size, `Assembler.nextNum`) and refuse a larger one
  (`error.SzxChanged` / `error.SzxIncrease`).
- **CoAP over TCP/TLS** (`tcp.zig`, RFC 8323 §3, §5). The stream framing (`serialize`, `decode`, `frameLen`: Len/TKL
  with the 0/1/2/4-octet extended length, no Version/Type/Message ID), the signaling messages (CSM with Max-Message-Size,
  Block-Wise-Transfer and Extended-Token-Length, Ping/Pong with Custody, Release with Alternative-Address and
  Hold-Off, Abort with Bad-CSM-Option) and `Session`, the per-connection state machine (CSM first, a second CSM or an
  Empty message is a protocol error, Ping answered by a Pong with the token, Release stops new exchanges, Abort closes).
  Decoding is bounded (`default_max_body` 1 MiB: the 4-octet length could announce 4 GiB). The TLS seam is the caller's,
  as for DTLS. The option and payload codec is the datagram one (`coap.parseBody` / `serializeBody`), so both framings
  share it. libcoap and go-coap implement the same sections.
- **RFC 9175 Echo and Request-Tag** (`echo.zig`). `EchoVerifier` is the stateless freshness challenge (§2.4/§2.6): the
  Echo value is the issue time plus a keyed HMAC-SHA-256 over time and peer identity (24 octets, within 1..40), checked in
  constant time and against a lifetime; `challenge` is the gate that answers 4.01 with a new Echo value or lets a fresh
  repeat through. `RequestTagTracker` is §3.3's server rule over caller storage: a Block1 block with NUM 0 starts an
  operation (replacing an unfinished one of the same peer and resource), later blocks must carry the same Request-Tag values in
  order and the next NUM, a retransmission of the previous block is accepted, anything else is `tag_mismatch` or
  `no_operation` (4.08); a full table is `full` (5.03). At most 4 tag values of 8 octets per operation.
- **Multicast** (`multicast.zig`, RFC 7252 §8). `requestAllowed` (Non-confirmable only), `leisureMs` (§8.2's
  `S * G / R`, 5 s default), `responseDelayMs` (uniform within the Leisure), `shouldAnswer` (only 2.xx; errors are
  dropped), the answer type (Non-confirmable) and the "All CoAP Nodes" addresses. The dispatcher's `multicast` flag
  already keeps unmatched discovery silent.

## Threat model / out of scope
CoAP itself is unauthenticated/unencrypted on the wire. This module is transport-agnostic — the
caller supplies the datagram transport, and that transport can be **any** of: plain UDP, or a
caller-terminated **DTLS** session (RFC 7252 §9 / RFC 7641 §8's mandated CoAP transport security).
There is no CoAP-specific DTLS integration here — the same BYO-transport seam this repo uses for
BYO-TLS on TCP — so wiring DTLS is purely a matter of handing this module's `parse`/`serialize`
plaintext datagrams from/to whatever authenticated channel the caller already runs. **Production
CoAP over an untrusted network MUST run over that DTLS seam**; plain UDP is only appropriate on an
already-trusted link (e.g. a private network). No congestion control beyond the §4.8 transmission
parameters. Within C6, a mid-transfer SZX change to a *larger* size is refused with a typed error
rather than mis-assembled (only a decrease is a renegotiation, RFC 7959 §2.3).

Four items are attacker-triggerable **on an unauthenticated, connectionless UDP transport**. The
first two are **bounded (admission hook + DTLS seam)**, the third is **NOT bounded here**, and the
fourth is bounded by a per-subscription budget the push path consults:

1. **Message-ID dedup window** (§4.5, `reliability.Dedup`) — caller-storage-bounded; an attacker who
   can inject packets can flood it with distinct message IDs to evict a legitimate exchange's entry
   before its retransmission window elapses, after which a replayed/retransmitted message with that
   ID is no longer recognized as a duplicate and is reprocessed. `Dedup`'s table size (the caller's
   storage slice) and remembered-duration (`lifetime_ms`) are caller-configurable — a
   deployment sizes both for its expected authenticated-peer/exchange count — but sizing alone
   doesn't change what kind of control this is: **`Dedup` is a reliability control (duplicate
   suppression), not a replay-security control.** It becomes a security boundary only once the
   *source* is authenticated, i.e. run over the DTLS seam above, so that flooding one peer's window
   requires being that peer. See `reliability.zig`'s `Dedup` doc comment.
2. **Observe subscription registry** (§C7, `observe.Registry`) FIFO-evicts the oldest subscription
   when full. `Registry` offers an **admission hook**: `admit_fn`/`admit_ctx` (type
   `observe.AdmitFn`, a plain function pointer + opaque context — no allocation, no closures) plus
   an optional **per-source cap** (`max_per_source`), both consulted by the `Registry.tryRegister`
   entry point (the unconditional `register` primitive is unchanged, for callers that gate admission
   themselves or trust their transport). A hook that returns `false`, or a source at its cap, is
   rejected *before* the table is touched — no eviction of any existing entry. `source_id` is the
   caller's opaque peer identity; it is only a meaningful admission signal when it comes from an
   authenticated source (again, the DTLS seam) — a hook keyed off the unauthenticated UDP source
   address is not a mitigation, since that address is trivially spoofed. See `observe.zig`'s module
   and `Registry` doc comments for the full API and its `tryRegister` tests.

3. **Response amplification** (RFC 7252 §11.3) — **not bounded by this module, and it cannot be.**
   `block.split` and `server.piggyback` make a large answer to a small question easy, and the UDP
   source address is chosen by whoever sends the datagram. Nothing here rate-limits, requires a
   round trip before a large response, or compares response size to request size. A deployment on
   an untrusted network gets that from the DTLS seam (a handshake the spoofer cannot complete), not
   from this layer.
4. **Observe notification volume** (RFC 7641 §7) — **bounded per subscription, on by default.**
   §7 is a MUST: "Without client authentication, a server therefore MUST strictly limit the number
   of notifications that it sends between receiving acknowledgements that confirm the actual
   interest of the client in the data; i.e., any notifications sent in non-confirmable messages
   MUST be interspersed with confirmable messages." `Registry`'s two admission controls —
   `admit_fn` and `max_per_source` — bound **how many rows of the table one source occupies**, not
   what a registration costs, which is the stream of notifications that follows it. That stream is
   bounded by `Registry.Entry.non_since_ack` + `last_ack_ms` and the push-path decision point
   `Registry.notificationType`: after `max_non_between_acks` non-confirmable notifications
   (default 5, libcoap's `COAP_OBS_MAX_NON` — §7 names no number) it returns `.confirmable` and
   keeps doing so until the caller reports an ACK through `Registry.acknowledged`; it also returns
   `.confirmable` once 24 hours have passed since the last one (§4.5, independent of the budget).
   `max_non_between_acks = null` switches the budget off, which §7 permits only for an
   authenticated client. The module still never sends anything: a caller that ignores
   `notificationType` is not bounded, which is why the push-path contract is in `observe.zig`'s
   module doc comment.
   Note also §7's closing sentence — "an attacker
   may still spoof the acknowledgements if the confirmable messages are sufficiently predictable".
   The confirmable messages it means are the server's notifications, and their ACK is normally an
   empty message echoing only the **Message ID** — so what has to be unpredictable is
   `server.Server.init`'s `seed_mid`, not the client's token (in the amplification attack the
   spoofer chose the token itself); `Server.init` and `Registry.acknowledged` state the CSPRNG
   requirement, and nothing here can test a seed's entropy. The
   registry binds the ACK to the CON's Message ID: `confirmableSent` records the id of the outstanding
   confirmable notification and `acknowledged` resets the budget only for that id (a stray, repeated,
   superseded or forged id changes nothing).

Items 1–2 remain properties of *unauthenticated* CoAP, not bugs in this codec/state-tracking layer: the
hook and cap bound what an *admitted* or *uncapped* misbehaving source can do, but the real fix for
an untrusted network is DTLS (peer authentication) terminated by the caller, feeding a real
`source_id` and `admit_fn` policy into `Registry.tryRegister`.

Known limit: `Registry.register`/`tryRegister` truncate a token longer than 8 octets to 8 (`coap.max_token_len`), so
`find` never matches such an entry and it can be neither notified, acknowledged nor cancelled;
`parse` rejects TKL > 8, so only a caller can supply one.

## Verification

- **Run:** `scripts/modtest coap` (offline).
- **Test classes:** codec (golden-byte CON GET round-trip, extended option nibbles at the 13/269 boundaries, payload-marker edge cases, the full parse/serialize error matrix, `encodedLen` agreement, the RFC 8974 extended forms); options (class bits, uint codec boundaries and round-trip, typed accessors, URI-to-options mapping with percent-encoding, `coaps`, bad scheme, a hostile Uri-Host escaped rather than emitted verbatim); reliability (retransmit schedule with jitter and full backoff to `timed_out`, `ack`/`onReset`, custom `max_retransmit`, the dedup window: fresh/duplicate/expiry/eviction, zero-length storage never panics); client/server (request assembly and counter advance, `Exchange.match` across all five reply kinds, `isRequest` gating, response builders, an end-to-end client-server-client round trip); block-wise (value codec edges, `split` boundary and `Assembler` completion, a lone high-`num` final block and a mid-stream gap rejected, a mid-transfer SZX change rejected, byte-exact 3000-byte Block2 GET reassembly, Block1 PUT with `2.31 Continue`); Observe (`Sequence` wrap and lollipop comparison, freshness-checked notify, FIFO eviction, re-register refresh, the `tryRegister` admission policy, the notification budget, end-to-end register/notify/stale-reject/cancel, CON-notification timeout and RST cancellation glue); link-format and resources (RFC 6690 §5 documents as exact writer bytes and parser input, the §4.1 filter examples, RFC 8132 §6, RFC 9175 table, RFC 7967 §2.1 and RFC 8974 §2.1 encodings as goldens, the dispatcher's method matrix and discovery).
- **External anchor** (`src/external_goldens.zig`): datagrams captured from real `aiocoap` 0.4.17 endpoints (an `aiocoap-client` and an `aiocoap.resource.Site` server) through a byte-logging UDP proxy: a plain GET, a full 3-block Block2 GET reassembly, a Block1 PUT with a chained Block1+Size1 option delta, an Observe registration followed by two live-pushed notifications (driving this module's `Registry`/`Sequence` with the real sequence numbers), and a multi-byte Block value from a 17-block transfer. This catches a convention wrong the same way on both sides of a self-round-trip (the `Block.encode`/`decode` byte order is the example in the file's doc comment). Limits of the anchor: both endpoints are one implementation, so a misreading of RFC 7252 inside `aiocoap` is invisible to it; every capture is a well-formed loopback CON/ACK exchange with TKL 2, so no golden exercises a refusal path (every `ParseError`, `Block.DecodeError` and `FormatError` branch is anchored by hand-authored tests alone); the captures are frozen bytes, re-taken by `tools/capture_goldens.py` (Message IDs and tokens are random per run, so its `--compare` mode checks that the options and payloads are identical). Observed difference, not a bug: `aiocoap-client` elides `Uri-Host` for a destination-matching IP literal (RFC 7252 §6.4 SHOULD); `options.optionsFromUri` never elides it. Attribution: root `NOTICE` §0 (black-box oracle, no source consulted).
- **Fuzz:** deterministic driver prefix `COAP_FUZZ` (`COAP_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]`; harness names `coap-<file>-<function>`): `coap-root-parse` (parse then serialize round-trip: the option-nibble encoding is canonical, so `serialize` of any accepted datagram reproduces it), `coap-linkformat-parse` (parser, filter and writer round-trip model) and `coap-resource-dispatch` (datagram, parse, dispatch, serialize); reach tests in the suite.
- **Mutation:** the whole-module run covers every runtime line of the nine source files. Not mutated, because the value is a comptime constant a runtime switch cannot reach: the option numbers, content-format ids, `default_max_age`, the default ports, `max_num`, `Methods.all`, the `Params` defaults. One pinned quirk: a non-default `Uri-Port` asks for an 8-byte scratch window although its value needs at most two bytes (tests pin 8 accepted, 7 refused).
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and the delta runs after it.

## What is deliberately not done

- **RFC 6690 `rel`, `anchor` and `rev` semantics** (context-URI resolution) are parsed, not interpreted: a resource
  directory or proxy needs them, a server that lists its own resources does not (RFC 6690 §2 leaves the interpretation
  to the application).
- **CoAP over WebSockets (RFC 8323 §4)** and **RFC 7390 group-management resources** (the JSON `/gm` documents): the
  first is an HTTP upgrade plus WebSocket framing around the same messages and belongs with an HTTP stack; the second is
  ordinary resource handling, with nothing to decode that `resource.zig` and a JSON module do not already cover.
- **Observe/Block hooks beyond the two above:** the dispatcher stays a pure function of one request; a handler that
  needs request-body assembly drives `block.Assembler` and `echo.RequestTagTracker` itself.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle MIXED

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle MIXED** — anchored for some paths, self for others — the evidence below names which.

**What the tests actually contain.** src/external_goldens.zig replays real aiocoap 0.4.17 client<->server datagrams captured through a byte-logging UDP proxy (plain GET, the full 3-pair Block2 transfer, Block1 PUT with a real Uri-Path/Block1/Size1 delta chain, a live Observe push, multi-byte Block NUM); options/reliability/server scheduling in root.zig stay hand-authored
